questions.explanation: Replication exists for latency (data near users), availability (survive node loss), and read throughput (more machines serving reads). It does not reduce storage — copies cost more storage — and it complicates consistency and failover rather than guaranteeing or simplifying them.
options: To reduce storage costs, simplify the schema, and speed up writes
To keep data geographically close to users, keep the system available during failures, and scale out read throughput
To eliminate the need for backups, transactions, and indexes
To guarantee strong consistency, reduce network traffic, and simplify failover
questions.question: Which of the following is the standard set of reasons for replicating data across multiple machines?

questions.explanation: Only the leader accepts writes; followers consume its replication log and must apply writes in the same order the leader processed them. Reads can be served by any replica — that is how replication scales read throughput. Followers never accept client writes and must preserve write order.
options: Clients send writes to any replica, and replicas gossip the changes among themselves
All writes go to the leader, which streams them to followers via a replication log; clients may read from the leader or any follower
Writes go to the leader, and all reads must also go to the leader to stay consistent
Followers apply the leader's writes in whatever order they arrive
questions.question: In single-leader (leader-based) replication, which statement is true?

questions.explanation: With async replication the leader doesn't wait for followers, so an acknowledged write may exist only on the dead leader and be lost. Synchronous replication would have prevented the loss (a follower holds a copy) but blocks writes whenever a follower stalls — which is why many systems use semi-synchronous replication as a compromise.
options: The write is safe because the leader acknowledged it
The acknowledged write can be permanently lost
Followers automatically roll the write forward from their own logs
All subsequent writes are blocked until a new leader is elected
questions.question: A database uses fully asynchronous replication. The leader acknowledges a write and crashes before forwarding it to any follower. What is the consequence?

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes means a client always sees its own updates; replication lag breaks it when reads hit a stale follower. Monotonic reads is about time appearing to move backward across successive reads, consistent prefix reads is about seeing causally related writes out of order, and write-write conflicts are a multi-leader problem — none match this scenario.
options: Violation of read-your-writes consistency
Violation of monotonic reads
Violation of consistent prefix reads
A write-write conflict
questions.question: A user changes their profile photo, reloads the page, and sees the old photo. The app reads from an asynchronous follower. Which consistency anomaly is this?

questions.explanation: Reading from the leader guarantees fresh data but concentrates all read load on one node — you lose the read-throughput scaling and the availability benefit of serving reads from followers. This is the core tension: stronger guarantees against lag cost you scalability and availability.
options: Writes become slower because the leader must wait for followers
The leader becomes a read bottleneck, giving up the read scalability and some availability that followers provided
Followers can no longer be used for disaster recovery
The system can no longer tolerate any follower failures
questions.question: To eliminate replication-lag anomalies, a team routes every read to the leader. What is the main cost of this fix?

questions.explanation: Each leader accepts writes locally without coordinating, so conflicting writes both succeed and the conflict is only discovered when the leaders replicate to each other asynchronously. This delayed detection is the fundamental price of multi-leader replication — unlike single-leader, where conflicts are impossible by construction.
options: Immediately — one of the writes is rejected at write time
Later and asynchronously, after both writes have already succeeded locally
During the next leader election
It can't happen; the leaders coordinate before accepting writes
questions.question: In multi-leader replication, two clients concurrently update the same record on two different leaders. When is the conflict detected?

questions.explanation: Read repair fixes stale replicas when a read observes disagreement, and anti-entropy is a background process that continuously compares replicas and syncs differences. Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff instead maximize write availability during a partition — they accept writes on stand-in nodes rather than reconciling stale data.
options: Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
Read repair and the anti-entropy process
Leader election and log truncation
Synchronous replication and fencing tokens
questions.question: After a network partition heals, some replicas in a Dynamo-style system hold stale values. Which pair of mechanisms converges them back into agreement?

questions.explanation: The three classic lag anomalies each have a standard fix: read-your-writes via leader reads after writes, monotonic reads by pinning each user to one replica, and consistent prefix reads by colocating causally related writes. Lag never causes writes to be rejected, and adding leaders doesn't fix stale reads — that's a different replication model entirely.
options: Not seeing your own recent write → route reads to the leader briefly after a write (or track the write's replication position)
Seeing time move backward across successive reads → always route a given user's reads to the same replica
Seeing causally related writes out of order → keep causally related writes on the same partition
Writes being rejected under load → add more leaders to the cluster
questions.question: Which anomaly-to-fix pairings for replication lag are correct? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Multi-datacenter deployments and offline/collaborative use cases are the two canonical reasons for multiple leaders. All-to-all topologies are the most fault-tolerant but can violate causal ordering. Multi-leader never eliminates write conflicts — concurrent writes to different leaders are its defining problem, and quorums are a leaderless-replication concept.
options: It fits multi-datacenter operation, with one leader per datacenter so writes stay local
It fits offline clients and collaborative editing, where each client acts as a leader and syncs later
In an all-to-all topology, causally related writes can arrive out of order at some replicas
It eliminates write conflicts because every write goes through a quorum of leaders
questions.question: Which statements about multi-leader replication are true? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: The real approaches are avoidance (a home leader per record), convergence via last-write-wins (simple but lossy, and vulnerable to clock skew), and merging (application logic, CRDTs, or asking the user). Blocking until all leaders acknowledge would destroy the availability multi-leader is chosen for, and it isn't a conflict-resolution strategy.
options: Avoid conflicts by routing all writes for a given record to the same designated leader
Converge with last-write-wins, accepting that some concurrent writes are silently discarded
Merge the conflicting values with application logic or CRDTs so no update is lost
Block each write until every leader has acknowledged it
questions.question: Which are legitimate strategies for handling write conflicts in multi-leader replication? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Leaderless writes go to all N replicas with W acknowledgments; W+R>N makes read and write quorums overlap so reads usually return the latest write; sloppy quorums plus hinted handoff trade consistency for write availability during partitions. But quorum overlap is not linearizability — concurrent writes, partial failures, and sloppy quorums all create edge cases, so it only makes reads probably fresh.
options: The client writes to all N replicas, and the write succeeds once W of them acknowledge it
When W + R > N, the read quorum overlaps the write quorum, so reads usually see the latest acknowledged write
With sloppy quorums, writes can go to reachable stand-in nodes during a partition and are handed back to the home replicas later (hinted handoff)
W + R > N guarantees linearizable reads and writes in all cases
questions.question: Which statements about Dynamo-style (leaderless) quorum replication are true? (Select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Single-leader is the default for most databases (conflict-free, failover needed); multi-leader buys local multi-datacenter writes and offline support with conflict resolution as the price; leaderless buys availability and tunable quorums with complexity and only eventual consistency. No strategy removes the fundamental tradeoff — replication always trades consistency, availability, and latency against each other.
options: Single-leader is the simplest default: no write conflicts by construction, but you must handle leader failover
Multi-leader suits multi-datacenter and offline use cases, at the cost of resolving write conflicts
Leaderless replication offers high availability and tunable consistency via quorums, at the cost of operational complexity and weaker guarantees
Adding more replicas removes the tradeoff between consistency, availability, and latency
questions.question: Which statements correctly summarize the chapter's guidance on choosing a replication strategy? (Select all that apply)

summary.overview: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple machines so data stays close to users, the system survives failures, and read load can scale out. The hard part isn't copying static data — it's keeping replicas in sync as data changes. This chapter compares three strategies for that problem — single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication — and shows how each trades off consistency, availability, and operational complexity.

sections.heading: Leaders and Followers
takeaways: Replicate for three reasons: lower latency (data near users), higher availability (survive node failures), and more read throughput (more machines serving reads).

Single-leader: every write goes to one leader, which records it locally and streams it to followers in a replication log; followers apply writes in the leader's order; clients can read from any replica but only the leader accepts writes.

Synchronous replication waits for follower confirmation (durable but a stalled follower blocks writes); asynchronous doesn't wait (fast and available but acknowledged writes can be lost on failover); semi-synchronous (one sync follower, rest async) is the common compromise.

sections.heading: Problems with Replication Lag
takeaways: Reading from lagging async followers causes three anomalies: missing your own recent write (read-your-writes), seeing time go backward across reads (monotonic reads), and seeing causally related writes out of order (consistent prefix reads).

Standard fixes: read-your-writes by reading from the leader briefly after a write (or tracking the write's position); monotonic reads by pinning each user to one replica; consistent prefix reads by writing causally related data to the same partition.
Stronger guarantees cost scalability and availability — e.g., routing all reads to the leader makes it a bottleneck, giving up the read scaling followers provide.

sections.heading: Multi-Leader Replication
takeaways: Multiple leaders each accept writes and replicate to each other; the main use cases are multi-datacenter operation (a local leader per datacenter) and offline clients / collaborative editing.
The price is write conflicts: the same record can be changed concurrently on two leaders, both succeed locally, and the conflict is discovered later, asynchronously.

Handle conflicts by avoidance (route each record's writes to one home leader) or convergence: last-write-wins (simple, silently discards data, clock-skew risk), merging values (application logic, CRDTs), or prompting the user.
Replication topology matters: star, circular, and all-to-all; all-to-all is the most fault-tolerant but can deliver causally related writes out of order.

sections.heading: Leaderless Replication
takeaways: Dynamo-style: no leader; the client (or coordinator) writes to all N replicas and the write succeeds after W acknowledgments; reads query R replicas and take the newest version.
Quorum rule: if W + R > N, the read set overlaps the write set, so reads usually see the latest acknowledged write (typical: N=3, W=2, R=2, tolerating one node failure).
Sloppy quorums boost write availability during partitions by accepting writes on reachable stand-in nodes; hinted handoff returns those writes to the home replicas once connectivity heals.
Replicas reconverge via read repair (fix stale copies when a read sees disagreement) and a background anti-entropy process that compares and syncs replicas.

Quorums are not linearizability: concurrent writes, partial write failures, and sloppy quorums mean reads are only probably fresh — concurrent writes still need resolution (e.g., last-write-wins or version vectors).

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Three strategies: single-leader (simplest, no write conflicts, needs failover), multi-leader (multi-datacenter/offline writes, write conflicts to resolve), leaderless (high availability, tunable consistency, operational complexity).

Choose by workload: single-leader is the default for most databases; multi-leader for multi-datacenter and offline use; leaderless when you need high availability and can tolerate eventual consistency.
Replication's core tension is unavoidable: keeping changing data in sync forces tradeoffs among consistency, availability, and latency.
